hook: Hospitals measure blood glucose, water labs measure nitrate, and food scientists check the dye in sports drinks by shining one color of light through a sample. The more of the colored substance there is, the more light it absorbs, in exact proportion.

prereq.q: What is the molarity of 0.0200 mol of solute in 0.500 L of solution?
A solution looks blue. Which light does it absorb most?
prereq.why: We see the light that is not absorbed.

figure.caption: Light of one wavelength passes through the sample; the instrument reports absorbance.

chain.cause: Each absorbing particle in the beam can absorb a photon of matching energy
chain.effect: more particles in the path absorb more light

chain.cause: Doubling the concentration or the path length doubles the particles in the beam
chain.effect: absorbance is proportional to both: A = εbc
measurements there are most sensitive to concentration

chain.cause: Standards of known concentration fall on a straight line of A against c
chain.effect: an unknown's absorbance on that line gives its concentration

ideas: A = εbc: A unitless, ε in L/(mol·cm), b in cm, c in mol/L.
Measure at λmax, the wavelength of maximum absorbance.
Calibration curve: A against c is a straight line through the origin with slope εb.
Errors that add absorbance (fingerprints, no blank) make the concentration too high.

misconception.wrong: A solution that absorbs more light must have a larger molar absorptivity.
misconception.right: ε is fixed for a substance at one wavelength. More absorbance at the same wavelength and path length means a higher concentration.

summary: A spectrophotometer measures how much light of one wavelength a solution absorbs. The Beer-Lambert law, A = εbc, makes absorbance proportional to concentration and path length. Measurements are made at λmax, and a calibration curve of standards gives an unknown's concentration; anything that adds absorbance, such as fingerprints or a missed blank, makes it read too high.
